item.title: HC dismisses rule over police security for housing project
item.description:
The High Court has dismissed a rule issued over police security for the implementation of the Purbachal Probashi Palli Limited housing project, after the state accused the writ petitioner of misusing the court’s interim order for personal gain.
Lawyers concerned confirmed the matter on Thursday.
The High Court bench of Justice Ahmed Sohel and Justice SM Iftekhar Uddin Mahmud pronounced the verdict.
According to the case documents, Mohammad Muhidur Rahman, managing director, and Habibur Rahman, chairman, established Purbachal Probashi Palli Limited in Dhaka’s Purbachal with funding from expatriates. The company was registered on December 31, 2009.
In 2011, the company filed a writ petition with the High Court seeking police security for its business activities.
Md Abdul Qayyum, the company’s project director, filed the petition under authority granted by the company. Nine people were made respondents, including the secretary of the Ministry of Home Affairs, the deputy commissioners and upazila nirbahi officers of Narayanganj and Narsingdi, the managing director of Purbachal American City Mohammad Abdullah Al Mamun, and the officers-in-charge of Rupganj and Narsingdi Sadar police stations.
Following the initial hearing on July 25, 2011, the High Court directed the OCs of Narsingdi Sadar and Rupganj police stations to provide necessary security for four months to prevent obstacles to the implementation of the project.
The court also issued a rule asking why the respondents’ failure to provide legal protection for the project should not be declared illegal and without lawful authority. It further asked why the respondents should not be directed to refrain from obstructing the lawful implementation of the project.
The company subsequently continued to operate its housing business by obtaining extensions of the four-month interim order from time to time over nearly 15 years.
Meanwhile, Sub-Inspector Ahsan Habib filed a response before the court on behalf of the OC of Rupganj police station, the ninth respondent in the case.
In the response filed on July 16, the state denied the allegations made in the writ petition. During the hearing, the state argued that the interim security order had been repeatedly extended and allegedly used for personal gain and fraudulent purposes for nearly 15 years.
The state told the court that the project was a privately owned commercial real estate and housing project whose legal approval and registration were themselves disputed.
It also said that in a case filed on September 11, 2024, under the anti-discrimination movement-related proceedings (GR Case No 154/2024), the project’s chairman Habibur Rahman and managing director Muhidur Rahman had been named as the first and 51st accused, respectively.
Despite this, the state argued that the project had continued to receive police security by relying on the 2011 High Court order.
The state further alleged that the project directors had forcibly taken possession of land belonging to farmers in several mouzas through fraud and forged documents. It said reports on the allegations had also been published in national newspapers.
The state argued that the original interim order in the writ had been misused to allegedly facilitate fraud and harass local landowners, while the institution itself lacked proper legal validity.
On these grounds, the state sought a penalty against the writ petitioner for allegedly filing the petition for personal gain.
After hearing both sides, the High Court dismissed the rule and delivered its verdict.
Following the verdict, the state’s lawyers said the writ petitioner had obtained a four-month interim order in 2011 and repeatedly extended it for nearly 15 years.
They alleged that the security order had been misused during this period and that the company had used it to pursue its own interests. They also alleged that the chairman and managing director, who were accused in a case related to the anti-discrimination movement, had used the High Court order to avoid arrest.
After considering the arguments, the High Court dismissed the rule issued in response to the writ petition.

item.title: Gold prices rise again
item.description:
After several rounds of price cuts, the Bangladesh Jewellers Association (Bajus) has raised gold prices again in the domestic market.
The price of 22-carat gold has been increased by Tk4,474 per bhori to Tk236,354, according to a Bajus announcement on Thursday.
The new price came into effect at 10am on Thursday.
Bajus said the new rates were set considering the overall market situation following an increase in the prices of acid gold and silver.
The decision was taken at a meeting of Bajus’s Standing Committee on Pricing and Price Monitoring on Thursday morning.
According to the new rates, 22-carat hallmarked gold costs Tk20,350 per gram, including VAT. The price of 21-carat gold has been set at Tk19,435 per gram, 18-carat gold at Tk16,685 per gram and traditional gold at Tk13,630 per gram.
Bajus has also increased the price of silver.
Under the new rates, 22-carat silver costs Tk440 per gram, 21-carat silver Tk425, 18-carat silver Tk365 and traditional silver Tk275 per gram.
Earlier, Bajus reduced the price of gold on Wednesday, September 2. The price of 22-carat gold was cut by Tk4,374 per bhori to Tk2,31,880.
Before that, Bajus reduced the price of 22-carat gold by Tk4,374 on August 31 and by Tk7,115 on August 29.
The latest increase comes just a day after the most recent price cut.
Bajus said labour charges would apply depending on the design of the jewellery. However, as VAT is already included in the selling price, jewellers cannot charge customers VAT separately.
For the exchange or purchase of gold and silver jewellery, Bajus’s existing rules will remain in effect, excluding applicable VAT, labour charges and stone prices.
The new rates will remain in effect at jewellery shops across the country until further notice.

item.title: Can we expect a better labour market?
item.description:
Malaysia’s labour market is set to reopen after a prolonged suspension marked by scrutiny, political transitions, and deep uncertainty.
For years, the recruitment of Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia has been surrounded by allegations of syndication, excessive recruitment costs, limited access to recruitment services, and practices that left workers bearing the greatest burden of a system over which they had little control.
During the tenure of Sheikh Hasina's government, the recruitment of Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia became increasingly entangled with political and business interests. The recruitment arrangements developed during this period are often linked to the emergence of a syndication model that would later concentrate access to the Malaysian labour market among a select group of agencies. What began under one set of political actors, however, did not end with them.
Over the years, other parliamentarians and politically-connected interests became part of the wider ecosystem, allowing the model to persist and evolve. The problem, therefore, cannot simply be reduced to one minister, one political party, or one period of government.
At its core was a recruitment structure in which access became concentrated, while aspiring migrant workers bore the consequences through high costs, uncertainty, and limited choice.
For Bangladeshi workers, these were never simply matters of policy or politics. They meant years of waiting, borrowing money, paying recruitment fees, and placing their hopes in a system that often seemed designed around everything except the worker.
The consequences became painfully visible on May 31, 2024, when hundreds of aspiring migrant workers gathered at Dhaka airport, waiting to leave for Malaysia. Their recruiting agencies had failed to provide their air tickets before the deadline set by the Malaysian government expired that day. Malaysia closed its labour market to Bangladeshi workers from June 1. It was yet another painful repetition of a cycle in which migrant workers were left to bear the consequences of decisions over which they had little control.
However, the long suspension also created something that had been missing for years: An opportunity to rethink the system.
As Bangladesh emerged from 15 years under the same ruling party and moved through a political transition towards a new governing arrangement, there was hope that reopening the Malaysian labour market could mean more than simply restarting recruitment. Perhaps this time, recruitment could be more transparent. Perhaps agencies would be selected according to clear and measurable standards rather than political or business connections. Perhaps workers would no longer have to pay disproportionate sums simply for the opportunity to work.
There was, in other words, room for change.
But now, as Malaysia prepares to reopen the market with a fresh list of 25 recruiting agencies, an uncomfortable question remains: Does changing the names on the list amount to changing the system?
If the selection process continues to rely on a limited pool of agencies without sufficiently examining their recruitment history, worker complaints, fee structures, treatment of migrants, and compliance with fair recruitment standards, then the underlying problem remains. The same concentration of power could simply return under a different configuration.
And if that happens, it will be the migrant worker who pays the price once again.
The lesson from the previous system should not simply be that too few agencies were involved. It should be that concentrating recruitment among a select group without strong safeguards and accountability creates the conditions for exploitation. The number of agencies matters, but so does how they are selected, monitored, and held accountable.
A credible reopening should therefore begin with transparent selection criteria. Agencies should be assessed not only on their licences or administrative capacity, but also on their track record in fair recruitment practices, worker protection, compliance with agreed recruitment costs, and grievance handling.
Workers should be able to understand what they are paying for, where their money is going, what employment has been promised to them, and where they can seek help when those promises are not honoured.
This also requires stronger accountability on both sides of the migration corridor. Bangladesh and Malaysia need mechanisms to monitor recruitment practices, address worker complaints, and ensure that agencies or employers who violate agreed standards face meaningful consequences. Fair recruitment cannot depend on goodwill alone; it requires systems capable of enforcing it.
Most importantly, recruitment should no longer be treated as a transaction in which the worker is simply the final commodity being moved between two labour markets. A worker is not merely a unit of labour to be recruited, transported, and placed. The recruitment process determines the debt they carry, the expectations they leave home with and, ultimately, the vulnerability they may face at their destination.
A reopened labour market will inevitably be welcomed as an opportunity for thousands of Bangladeshis seeking employment abroad. It should be. Malaysia has long been an important destination for Bangladeshi workers, and legitimate employment opportunities can transform the lives of families.
But reopening the labour market cannot become the destination in itself.
The real test will come after the first worker leaves Bangladesh: How much did they pay? How accurately did the job match the promise? What protection did they receive? And who will stand beside them if something goes wrong?
If the answers remain unchanged, then we have not reopened a labour market; we have simply reopened an old system.
For years, Bangladeshi migrant workers have carried the cost of recruitment failures through debt, deception, uncertainty, and lost opportunities. They deserve more than a new list of recruiting agencies. They deserve a recruitment system in which transparency is the rule, accountability is enforceable, and dignity is treated as a condition of migration, not an afterthought.
Efrita Jahan is currently part of the BRAC Migration Program.

item.title: Are we asking the right questions about climate migration?
item.description:
Climate migration is no longer a distant phenomenon or a future concern; it is already reshaping communities, economies, and urban areas across the world.
Due to its unique geographic location, Bangladesh remains particularly vulnerable to adverse climate hazards. Every year, people affected by both slow and sudden events - including uneven precipitation, droughts, flash floods, cyclones, salinity intrusion, river erosion, and other environmental pressures -- leave their homes in search of livelihood opportunities elsewhere.
As these events continue to intensify, climate migration is increasingly becoming a development challenge. However, while considerable attention is being given to identifying climate migrants and estimating their numbers, far less attention is being paid to a more pressing question: How should Bangladesh prepare its towns and cities to manage increasing climate-linked mobility?
The lack of an agreed definition remains one of the most debated issues in climate migration discourse. The International Organization for Migration (IOM) defines climate migration as the movement of people who are compelled, or choose, to leave their habitual place of residence because of sudden or gradual environmental changes associated with climate change.
International frameworks have taken different approaches to understanding climate-related mobility. For example, the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) refers to climate change-induced displacement, migration, and planned relocation rather than relying on a specific definition of “climate migrant.”
This reflects the complexity of migration decisions, which are often shaped by multiple and overlapping environmental, economic, social, and political factors, making it difficult to attribute mobility solely to climate change.
Despite the ongoing debate over definitions, the scale of climate-linked mobility continues to grow.
According to the World Bank’s latest Groundswell report, more than 216 million people could move within their own countries by 2050 due to climate change. Bangladesh alone could experience as many as 19.9 million internal climate migrants by mid-century.
A joint assessment conducted by the Bangladesh government and IOM in 2025 estimates that nearly five million people are currently living in situations of internal displacement linked to natural disasters.
Whatever the exact number of climate-linked displaced persons today or in the coming decades, people are already moving, and Bangladesh must prepare for the consequences.
Most climate-affected households, particularly displaced populations, relocate within the country, often to nearby secondary towns and urban centres. A significant number eventually move to major cities.
According to the Migration Policy Institute, approximately 400,000 people arrive in Dhaka every year. However, migration decisions are rarely driven by a single factor.
Climate and environmental pressures often interact with economic opportunities, social networks, access to services, and other considerations in shaping mobility decisions.
Migration does not necessarily end vulnerability. Many migrants or displaced households settle in informal settlements where housing conditions are poor and access to services remains limited.
Men who once relied on agriculture, fishing, or other rural occupations usually become day labourers because their existing skills do not match the demands of urban labour markets.
Women often enter low-paid domestic work or other informal sectors. Economic hardship pushes many children into labour, compromising their education and limiting their future opportunities.
The consequences of climate-linked displacement and migration are beyond livelihoods and often impacts kinship, neighbourhood feelings, weakens community support systems, and creates psychological stress.
Drawing on Arjun Appadurai’s concept “capacity to aspire,” climate displacement affects not only the people’s circumstances but limits their capacity to imagine a better future.
When households become trapped in daily wages for survival, their ability to pursue long-term aspirations is diminished. Yet mental health and psychosocial wellbeing remain largely overlooked in climate migration discussions.
At the same time, receiving cities and towns face increasing pressures in managing water supply, sanitation, healthcare, education, housing, transportation, waste management, and other essential services for growing populations, often with limited financial and institutional capacities.
Climate migration therefore is not only a humanitarian issue; it is equally an urban governance and development challenge.
Recognising these realities, the government of Bangladesh adopted the National Strategy on Internal Displacement Management in 2021. Development partners, international organizations, NGOs, and research institutions have also invested considerable effort in responding to climate-linked migration.
However, one aspect of the current discussion deserves closer attention.
Increasingly, municipal authorities, development partners, and researchers seek to identify climate migrants and estimate their numbers in specific towns and cities.
While understanding population movements is important for planning services, infrastructure, and future urban growth, it is important to distinguish between estimating population movements and categorizing individuals as climate migrants.
Estimating population movements supports planning; labelling individuals as climate migrants raises practical and policy concerns.
Migration and displacement are often shaped by a combination of environmental, economic, social, demographic, and personal considerations. A family displaced by river erosion, for example, may also move in search of livelihood opportunities or to join relatives already living in urban areas.
Likewise, even when displacement follows a cyclone, such movement may also reflect governance failure, including weak embankment management, poor water management, and inadequate investment in local adaptation.
This complexity makes identifying an individual as a climate migrant or climate-displaced person far from straightforward.
The question is not whether climate change contributes to displacement and migration, but whether mobility can be attributed to climate factors alone.
This is particularly important because the global debate on climate migration extends beyond human mobility to encompass issues of shared responsibility, national adaptation efforts, development financing, and differing positions among industrialised, developing and least developed countries regarding greenhouse gas emissions.
Furthermore, even if the UNFCCC were to adopt a universally accepted definition of climate migration tomorrow, practical challenges would remain unresolved at the domestic level.
How would authorities distinguish climate migration from movement driven by economic necessity, social networks, family-related factors, or governance failures?
More importantly, it is worth asking what practical benefit such categorization would bring. While identifying climate migrants may be necessary in certain circumstances to facilitate targeted support and protection, categorization alone does not improve livelihoods or guarantee access to services.
Even if climate migrants could be identified with complete accuracy, the more fundamental challenge would remain unchanged: Whether local economies, urban systems, and public institutions are capable of accommodating increasing population movements in an inclusive and sustainable manner.
The challenge is not merely identifying people on the move, but ensuring that towns and cities are prepared to absorb them through adequate jobs, housing, infrastructure, and public services.
Without such capacities, a label by itself offers little practical value.
This is not an argument against data. Reliable estimates of population movement remain essential for planning and policymaking.
The argument is simply that counting people and labelling people are not the same thing. For planning purposes, we need to estimate people. For governance purposes, we need to serve people.
The more relevant policy question is not whether an individual can be conclusively identified as a climate migrant. Rather, it is whether local institutions, urban systems, and public services are capable of responding to increasing population movements in an inclusive and sustainable manner.
The discussion therefore needs to move beyond identifying climate migrants and towards strengthening the capacity of towns and cities to manage increasing population movements.
Climate-related mobility is inherently a multi-sectoral issue. Housing, healthcare, livelihoods, water supply, sanitation, waste management, and education cannot be addressed in isolation.
Rather, they require coordinated planning, investment, and institutional readiness to ensure that growing populations can be accommodated in a sustainable manner.
Strengthening local economies and creating opportunities beyond a few major cities can also help secondary cities absorb additional populations more effectively.
Urban planning should therefore anticipate future population movements and consider the additional demand for services, infrastructure, housing, and employment that may emerge over time.
Such investments will not only support people who move but also benefit existing residents and the wider urban ecosystem.
In the longer term, strengthening the capacity of secondary towns may contribute to a more balanced economic opportunities, public services, and investments across the country.
As climate impacts intensify in the coming decades, human mobility will become an increasingly important feature of Bangladesh’s development landscape.
The debate over definitions and classifications will undoubtedly continue. The important question therefore is whether Bangladesh is adequately preparing its towns and cities to manage increasing climate migrants in a way that supports both people and places.
Md Abul Basar is an Anthropologist and Governance Expert, serving as Team Leader at Swisscontact Bangladesh, a Switzerland-based international organization. He can be reached at abul.basar@swisscontact.org.

item.title: Before the Earth moves
item.description:
The earthquake tragedy in Colombia last month should make Bangladesh ask a question that has little to do with predicting earthquakes: What happens when most of a nation's population, opportunity, and institutional capacity become concentrated in one city?
The United Nations projects Dhaka to become the world's largest city by 2050, with a population exceeding 50 million. Bangladesh already struggles with congestion, housing shortages, groundwater stress, pollution, inadequate sanitation, and enormous pressure on public services. Add tens of millions of people to this urban system, and earthquake vulnerability becomes only one dimension of a much larger human-development challenge.
Bangladesh already has projects designed to strengthen secondary cities, transportation corridors, and areas outside Dhaka. But the scale of the coming transformation requires something larger.
We should stop thinking primarily about moving people and start moving opportunities.
Start with those whose jobs may not survive
Walk through Dhaka and one sees an extraordinary amount of human effort.
A rickshaw puller pedals through extreme heat. A day labourer waits each morning hoping someone needs him. A young graduate rides a bicycle for deliveries because he cannot find work matching his education. A garment worker wonders whether automation will eventually replace part of her job. A rural worker leaves home because Dhaka appears to offer the only realistic path toward higher income.
These people are often described statistically as “labour.”
They are something much more important: Bangladesh's human capital.
The question is whether Bangladesh will continue using millions of people in occupations producing relatively little economic value and offering limited upward mobility or invest in enabling those same people to build the next economy.
Consider the rickshaw puller. The policy objective should not be to ban his rickshaw. That simply destroys income.
Ask instead: What could this person be doing 10 years from now?
Could he become a construction technician? A plumber? A logistics worker? A solar installer? A water-treatment operator? An emergency-response worker?
Then ask the more important question: What would it take to get him there?
That is human development.
Bangladesh may need housing and infrastructure for tens of millions of additional urban residents over the coming decades.
That sounds like a burden. It could also represent one of the largest employment opportunities in the country's history.
Building a network of 20 or 30 major economic centres would require enormous numbers of electricians, plumbers, welders, machine operators, construction workers, engineers, drivers, healthcare workers, water technicians, teachers, maintenance workers, and logistics professionals, among countless others.
Bangladesh already has much of the labour. The challenge is transforming skills.
Imagine a national program under which workers in vulnerable or low-productivity occupations receive paid training for three to 12 months. Training would be tied directly to employment.
The worker would not receive a certificate and then be told to search for a job. Infrastructure contracts receiving public support would commit to hiring qualified graduates.
The pathway becomes: Informal work → training → skilled employment → stable income → housing → financial inclusion → family security.
Urbanization then becomes a mechanism for social mobility.
Don't build another Dhaka
The objective should not be to create another megacity containing 30 million people.
Bangladesh needs a network.
Imagine economic centres distributed along existing and future rail, highway, and river corridors.
Some could specialize in healthcare and pharmaceuticals. Others in advanced textiles, food processing, logistics, electronics, renewable energy, technology, or light manufacturing.
Each would combine employment with housing, hospitals, schools, universities, parks, public transportation, and digital infrastructure.
That distinction is essential.
People do not move because planners draw circles on maps. They move because they can build better lives.
A family will leave Dhaka voluntarily when another city offers a good job, affordable home, safe school, reliable hospital, clean water, and reasonable transportation.
Bangladesh should therefore not attempt to redistribute population. It should redistribute reasons for people to choose where they live.
Water must come before homes
Water security should determine where these new centres grow.
Dhaka illustrates what happens when population growth outruns environmental infrastructure. The World Bank's current Metro Dhaka Water Security and Resilience Program describes serious pollution of rivers and canals resulting from rapid urbanization, inadequate sanitation, industrial discharge, and waste.
Bangladesh cannot sustainably replicate this pattern across the country. The next generation of cities should reverse the sequence.
Before approving hundreds of thousands of apartments, establish where their water will come from. Protect wetlands. Build reservoirs. Capture rainwater. Treat sewage. Recycle wastewater for industry. Protect groundwater recharge. Separate stormwater from sewage. Monitor industrial discharge digitally.
Bangladesh is one of the most water-rich landscapes on Earth, yet millions of citizens still experience problems involving safe drinking water.
That paradox demonstrates that water security is not merely about how much water a country possesses. It is about whether infrastructure delivers clean water to people when and where they need it.
Urban policy is health policy
The benefits would extend directly into national health.
A hospital treats disease after it occurs. A well-designed city can prevent some disease before the patient reaches the hospital.
Clean water reduces waterborne illness. Modern sanitation reduces exposure to pathogens. Cleaner transportation improves air quality. Better drainage reduces stagnant contaminated water. Trees and shaded streets reduce dangerous heat exposure. Walkable communities encourage physical activity. Shorter commutes give parents more time to their children. Formal employment makes health insurance and retirement savings more achievable. Distributed medical centres reduce the need for families across Bangladesh to travel to Dhaka for treatment.
For a country with limited healthcare resources, prevention through better living conditions may be among the highest-return health investments available.
Then there is the earthquake.
The magnitude-7.4 earthquake that struck Colombia last month demonstrated again how quickly buildings, roads, and ordinary lives can be transformed by seismic disaster.
Bangladesh cannot know exactly when a major earthquake will strike the region. But Dhaka's vulnerability is well documented.
The answer cannot simply be more ambulances and rescue equipment.
If tens of millions of people, major hospitals, government institutions, financial organizations, and businesses remain concentrated within the same metropolitan region, Bangladesh is effectively concentrating national risk.
Developing multiple economic centres is therefore similar to diversifying an investment portfolio. If one region suffers catastrophe, the country continues functioning. Decentralization becomes national insurance.
Give Dhaka room to breathe
This strategy does not require abandoning Dhaka. It may be the best way to save it.
As future population growth increasingly occurs elsewhere, Dhaka can begin repairing the damage created by decades of uncontrolled expansion.
Unsafe buildings can gradually be replaced. Canals can be restored. Wetlands can be protected. Emergency roads can be widened. Schools and hospitals can be retrofitted. Waterways can again become environmental assets rather than drains.
Dhaka could become safer without becoming economically irrelevant.
The objective is not to weaken Dhaka. It is to make Bangladesh stronger than Dhaka alone.
Dr Mazher Mir is a Bangladeshi writer with over three decades of work on socio-economic and human development issues.

item.title: Getting unfit buses off our roads
item.description:
That authorities are now saying unfit, or “rickety,” buses will not be allowed to operate, even when they possess fitness certificates, is certainly a welcome development, on paper.
For years, Dhaka’s commuters have been forced to share the roads with buses that are simply not fit to be called roadworthy -- with common defects like rusting bodies, broken windows, worn-out tires, faulty doors, and poorly maintained engines.
But while the acknowledgement of the problem is encouraging, this is a promise we have heard before.
The real problem is not a lack of rules: Bangladesh already has laws and regulatory mechanisms requiring vehicles to meet minimum safety standards; the glaring failure has always been enforcement.
A bus that is visibly unsafe should never have been on the roads in the first place. Additionally, if a vehicle deteriorates after receiving certification, there must be mechanisms to identify it and take it off the road.
This is why the latest initiative must go beyond occasional drives and headline-making announcements.
Fitness certificates must reflect the actual condition of vehicles rather than becoming a formality. Officials responsible for approving unsafe buses must also face accountability.
At the same time, bus owners need practical facilities and sufficient time to carry out repairs -- particularly as authorities move maintenance activities towards the planned Purbachal depot.
The reported plan to develop the facility is encouraging, but infrastructure must translate into better maintenance standards, not merely relocation.
Most importantly, enforcement cannot stop after the initial crackdown. Owners must know that an unsafe bus will be taken off the road -- regardless of its paperwork, influence, or age.
Dhaka’s commuters have waited long enough. We have heard these promises before. Now it is time to get it done and, more importantly, to ensure that the rules are strictly and consistently followed.

item.title: Going beyond relief for the Rohingya
item.description:
For about a decade, Bangladesh has carried an enormous humanitarian responsibility by sheltering hundreds of thousands of Rohingya refugees who fled persecution in Myanmar -- a feat that has proven to be both commendable and challenging.
While the ultimate solution remains their safe, dignified, and sustainable repatriation, the reality is that their displacement has continued for far too long. In such circumstances, ensuring that the Rohingya have opportunities to build skills and prepare for a better future is both practical and humane.
The newly launched skills development program for 1,000 Rohingya in Cox’s Bazar is, therefore, a welcome initiative.
With training in areas including tailoring, dressmaking, block printing, batik, mobile phone servicing, gas burner repair, and climate-smart agriculture, alongside essential soft skills, the program can help participants become more self-reliant and better prepared for future livelihood opportunities.
This is especially important because humanitarian assistance, while essential, cannot be the only focus when a crisis becomes prolonged. Aid can keep people alive and meet immediate needs, but skills, education, and livelihood opportunities can provide people with dignity, confidence, and the capacity to rebuild their lives.
For Bangladesh -- which continues to shoulder significant social, economic, and environmental pressures from hosting the Rohingya -- programs such as this also demonstrate that supporting the refugees does not have to mean simply providing relief.
We can, within the limitations of the camp environment and existing regulations, help prepare a generation for a future beyond dependency.
At the same time, such initiatives must complement and not replace the international community’s responsibility to resolve the crisis.
Bangladesh cannot be expected to host the Rohingya indefinitely. Greater international pressure must be maintained on Myanmar to create conditions for safe and dignified repatriation.
Until that becomes possible, however, it is a wise idea to do some good for the community’s future. Skills development is an investment in people, and the Rohingya surely deserve that.

item.title: 30 accused, including Sheikh Hasina, ordered to surrender
item.description:
The International Crimes Tribunal has ordered 30 accused, including ousted former prime minister Sheikh Hasina, former army chief General Aziz Ahmed and former inspector general of police Benazir Ahmed, to surrender to the tribunal by September 16.
The order came in a case filed over alleged crimes against humanity in connection with the Shapla Chattar massacre.
A newspaper notice has been issued in this regard.
The judicial panel of Tribunal-2, headed by Chairman Justice Nazrul Islam Chowdhury, passed the order on Thursday following a prosecution petition.
Earlier in the morning, the accused who are currently in custody were brought to the tribunal in prison vans amid tight security.
Eleven accused were scheduled to be produced before the tribunal on August 16. However, the prosecution sought more time, saying production warrants had not been issued against two of the accused and the non-execution reports (NERs) concerning those against whom arrest warrants had been issued had not been received.
The tribunal subsequently fixed Thursday for the proceedings.
On July 27, Tribunal-2 took cognizance of the formal complaint filed by the prosecution against 41 accused. It also issued arrest warrants against the absconding accused and ordered those in custody to be produced before the tribunal.
The case involves two charges. The first relates to the alleged killing of 32 people at Shapla Chattar in Dhaka’s Motijheel on May 5, 2013, during a Hefazat-e-Islam rally.
The second charge relates to alleged killings in different parts of the country, including the deaths of 20 people in Siddhirganj, Narayanganj, on May 6, 2013.

item.title: PM joins Janmashtami greetings program with Hindu community
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday joined a program to exchange greetings with prominent members of the Hindu community on the occasion of Janmashtami and to distribute honorariums among priests and sebaits.
The prime minister walked from his office at Bangladesh Secretariat to Osmani Memorial Auditorium in the capital to attend the Janmashtami programme as the chief guest at 10am.
The Ministry of Religious Affairs and the Hindu Religious Welfare Trust jointly organised the program, which is being attended by leading representatives of the Hindu community, religious leaders, eminent citizens, and priests and sebaits from different parts of the country.

item.title: Dhaka air quality remains ‘unhealthy for sensitive groups’
item.description:
Dhaka ranked 10th among the world’s cities with the worst air quality on Thursday morning, recording an Air Quality Index (AQI) score of 106 at 9:42am.
According to the AQI scale, the city's air quality was classified as “unhealthy for sensitive groups”, posing health risks to children, older adults, and people with heart or lung diseases, while the general public is mostly unaffected.
Kuching in Malaysia topped the global pollution list with an AQI of 274, followed by Kampala in Uganda with 16q and Jakarta in Indonesia with 158.
An AQI reading of 101 to 150 is considered "unhealthy for sensitive groups", while 151 to 200 is classified as "unhealthy". A reading between 201 and 300 is considered "very unhealthy", and anything above 301 is categorized as "hazardous", posing serious health risks.
The AQI provides a daily indication of air quality by measuring the level of pollution and its potential impact on human health.
In Bangladesh, the AQI is calculated based on five major pollutants — particulate matter (PM10 and PM2.5), nitrogen dioxide (NO2), carbon monoxide (CO), sulfur dioxide (SO2) and ozone.
Dhaka has long faced serious air pollution problems, with air quality generally deteriorating during the winter months and improving during the monsoon season.
The World Health Organization estimates that air pollution contributes to around 7 million deaths worldwide every year, mainly from stroke, heart disease, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, lung cancer and acute respiratory infections.

item.title: Kane scores twice as Bayern begins German Cup defense with 4-1 win
item.description:
Harry Kane scored twice as defending champion Bayern Munich comfortably advanced to the second round of the German Cup with a 4-1 victory over second-division Osnabrück on Wednesday.
Germany star Jamal Musiala was not included in Bayern's squad as he remained sidelined after collapsing during two preseason matches because of a neurological issue.
Bayern coach Vincent Kompany said Musiala “might” be available for Saturday's Bundesliga match against promoted Schalke.
“But I don't want to put any more pressure on the guy,” Kompany said.
Kompany opted against making major changes for the match against the lower-division side, starting star forwards Kane, Luis Diaz and Michael Olise. New signing Ismael Saibari also made his first start since joining Bayern from PSV Eindhoven.
Osnabrück took an early lead through a spectacular strike by Robin Meissner, who fired the ball into the top right corner from about 30 meters. Kane and even Bayern goalkeeper Jonas Urbig congratulated Meissner for the goal.
Kane equalized shortly afterward before Tom Bischof put Bayern ahead 2-1 in the 24th minute.
Bayern had to wait until the 73rd minute for Olise to extend its lead and effectively settle the contest.
Kane then completed the scoring from the penalty spot as Bayern began its defense of the German Cup with a comfortable victory.

item.title: US Open under the influence: content creators spark debate
item.description:
Jessica Pegula is all in favor of bringing more fans into tennis, but the world number three said Wednesday it's important to keep the focus on the game.
The US Tennis Association doubled down this year on credentials awarded to content creators -- reportedly handing out almost 100 after making 54 available in 2025 to amplify the tournament's presence on social media.
The influencers focus not just on tennis, but on fashion, food and lifestyle topics that are now an inextricable part of the game.
But the embrace of content creators sparked some backlash when the chair umpire of Naomi Osaka's first round match against Anastasia Zakharova had to shush a group in a courtside suite who appeared to be conducting a noisy photo shoot during a point.
"I think I can appreciate, you know, the influencers coming and kind of showcasing the US Open experience," Pegula said.
"I think that's something that the US Open has utilized a lot as far as food and drinks and things to do and the shops. That part is part of a fan experience and something that people might not know and make them want to go.
"But I do think that it's tough when you see videos like that, when they're taking pictures and using the selfie lights.
"People are down there trying to perform, and it's their career and their job. It seems a bit disrespectful," Pegula concluded.
Russian Daniil Medvedev, a former world number one and the 2021 US Open champion, said the more focus on the sport the better, and any problems can be ironed out.
"In general, the more the sport grows, the better it is," Medvedev said.
"For sure, if it disturbs during the play, like if you see the light or something, well, you always say to the referee.
"(It) can be sometimes challenging, like if during the point this happens. But I'm pretty sure as well, even them, you know, maybe one time they do it, and then someone tells them not to do it.
"I think (there is) a lot of more upside than downside, so go for it."

item.title: Alcaraz believes 'impossible' schedule raising injury threat
item.description:
Carlos Alcaraz said Wednesday he plans to play fewer tournaments in future, blaming an "impossible" tennis calendar for a rising number of injuries in the sport.
Alcaraz, who has only just returned from a four-month layoff caused by a wrist injury, was speaking after he moved into the third round of the US Open with a four-set defeat of Portugal's Jaime Faria.
The reigning US Open champion overcame a sluggish start before defeating his 72nd-ranked opponent 4-6, 6-0, 6-3, 6-2 in 2hr 40 min at the Arthur Ashe Stadium.
Afterwards the seven-time Grand Slam champion said while he had not wanted to spend four months on the sidelines this season, he planned to make regular breaks a part of his schedule in future.
"Obviously I don't want to have this break because an injury," the Spaniard said. "But in the future I'm going to take some breaks, some long breaks. Maybe not four months, but one month, two months, missing some tournaments, because it's impossible to play them all."
"I think they adding more important tournaments... you know, in a way they are making us play. You can say no.
"So it's impossible, and we are seeing a lot of players getting injured, a lot of players getting tired. If they don't do anything about it, we are going to see even more in the future.
"For me, taking this break because an injury, it wasn't that good, but you know, what I'm going to say is I'm going to take some breaks and missing some tournaments in the future, for sure."
Alcaraz showed some signs of rust against Faria, blaming his first set problems on a failure to convert a golden break point opportunity that would have given him a 4-2 lead.
Instead, Faria leveled at 3-3 and then broke Alcaraz in the next game to go 4-3 up.
"Tough match for me. Obviously the first set I was feeling great, I had break point, I missed it," Alcaraz said.
"After that I was in a rush. I didn't take time, I wasn't patient and that obviously cost me the break."
Faria was left ruing his inability to build on an impressive opening set. The 23-year-old's serve fell apart in the second while Alcaraz upped the tempo and began to find a telling extra zip in his groundstrokes.
Although Alcaraz had to save two break points in the opening game before holding, it was all one-way traffic thereafter.
Faria was broken three times as Alcaraz went through the gears to take control of the contest.
The Spaniard's momentum extended into the third set, with Faria broken again to go 2-0 down.
Faria hit back with a break of Alcaraz's serve to make it 2-1, but was soon back in trouble after being broken in the next game to trail 3-1.
The set went with serve thereafter as Alcaraz took a 2-1 lead.
Alcaraz went a double break up in the fourth to move into a 5-1 lead and served out to seal victory.

item.title: Man City, Chelsea fuel record-breaking Premier League transfer window
item.description:
Manchester City launched a new era by setting a Premier League transfer window record, while Chelsea made Morgan Rogers the most expensive British player in history.
Tottenham also embarked on a spending spree, but champions Arsenal missed out on a marquee forward and Liverpool and Manchester United may not have done enough.
After Premier League clubs broke their summer transfer record by spending £3.49 billion ($4.7 billion) before the window shut on Tuesday, AFP Sport looks at the key talking points:
Pep Guardiola's exit after a glorious decade as Manchester City manager sparked a major overhaul by his successor Enzo Maresca.
Maresca smashed the Premier League record for a single transfer window by spending £458 million on a host of new faces in a bid to reestablish City as England's preeminent force.
City have failed to win the title for the last two seasons and, with Rodri, John Stones, Bernardo Silva, Savio and Tijjani Reijnders among the recent departures, the club's Abu Dhabi powerbrokers responded by flexing their financial muscle.
Argentina midfielder Enzo Fernandez was prised from Chelsea for £125 million -- equalling the record fee paid by a British club -- while Nottingham Forest midfielder Elliot Anderson arrived for £116 million.
Everton winger Iliman Ndiaye was signed for £65 million, with Lille's Morocco teenager Ayyoub Bouaddi costing £85 million.
Chelsea might have lost Fernandez but new boss Xabi Alonso still spent £349 million to reinvigorate a team that finished 10th last season.
England midfielder Morgan Rogers arrived from Aston Villa for £117 million, while Maxence Lacroix, Emiliano Martinez, Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson are all proven Premier League performers.
Winners in dynamic fashion in their opening two matches this season, could Chelsea be on the verge of a title charge?
Already installed as the bookmakers' favourites for the Premier League crown, Arsenal were hoping to add a marquee forward in their bid for the club's first back-to-back English top-tier titles since the 1930s.
Interest in Real Madrid's Brazil winger Vinicius Junior and Atletico Madrid striker Julian Alvarez ultimately failed to end in a deal for either.
But Gunners boss Mikel Arteta, bolstered by the signings of Bruno Guimaraes, Ezri Konsa and Christos Tzolis, has little reason to fret, as his team proved by starting their title defence with consecutive wins.
At the other end of the Seven Sisters Road, big-spending Tottenham could not afford to be as measured as bitter rivals Arsenal in the transfer market.
Desperate to avoid a repeat of last season's relegation battle, Spurs lavished more than £300 million on new signings.
Italy midfielder Sandro Tonali, a £100 million capture from Newcastle, was the biggest of those deals, while Roberto De Zerbi brought in Chelsea duo Mykhailo Mudryk and Tosin Adarabioyo to make it 10 arrivals since the end of last season.
Yet, on the evidence of Tottenham's defeats by Brentford and Newcastle, De Zerbi's rebuild is very much a work in progress.
Heeding Andoni Iraola's plea for more wingers, Liverpool splashed £123 million on Paris Saint-Germain forward Bradley Barcola, but even that eye-catching move was not enough to convince many fans of their title credentials.
Iraola is in his first season in charge at Anfield after arriving from Bournemouth to replace the sacked Arne Slot following last season's disappointing fifth-placed finish.
Although the Reds have landed Barcola, French defender Jeremy Jacquet and Spanish winger Victor Munoz since last term, the departures of Mohamed Salah, Andrew Robertson and Ibrahima Konate have left questions about their ability to catch Arsenal.
Manchester United ended last season on a positive note, but the goodwill from their third-place finish under Michael Carrick is in danger of ebbing away following a quiet transfer window.
Youri Tielemans, Andrey Santos and Carlos Baleba have arrived to improve Carrick's central midfield options, but United look to have flaws at the back and in attack.
While Marcus Rashford's return from a loan at Barcelona could fix United's issues up front, their opening-weekend defeat at Hull was a damning indictment of their defensive problems.

item.title: Liton captain as BCB names men’s squad for Asian Games 2026
item.description:
Liton Das will lead Bangladesh as they compete against Asia’s finest cricketing sides at the Asian Games 2026.
Bangladesh Cricket Board (BCB) named the 15-member squad for the men’s tournament starting September 17.
The squad sees the return of major names from the one that played against Zimbabwe in July including the likes of captain Litton Das and Najmul Hossain Shanto.
The team had secured a podium finish, winning the bronze medal at the previous edition of the Asian Games, only behind Sri Lanka and India, who won the silver and gold medal respectively.
Bangladesh, along with India, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and Afghanistan, had secured automatic qualification for the tournament alongside the hosts Japan.
Nepal, Malaysia, Hong Kong, China and Oman had booked their slot following the qualifier tournament.
Bangladesh squad: Liton Das (c), Tanzid Hasan, Parvez Hossain Emon, Mohammed Saif Hasan, Najmul Hossain Shanto, Tawhid Hridoy, Musaddek Hossain Saikat, Yasir Ali Chowdhury, Rishad Hossain, Shak Mahedi Hasan, Nasum Ahmed, Mohammed Saifuddin, Shoriful Islam, Mustafizur Rahman, Hasan Mahmud.

item.title: Brazil-Japan to play World Cup rematch at Singapore tournament
item.description:
Japan will get a chance to avenge their heart-breaking World Cup defeat to Brazil when they take part in a four-team international tournament in Singapore in November, organisers said Thursday.
Gabriel Martinelli scored in the final moments in Houston to give Brazil a 2-1 win and knock out Hajime Moriyasu's side at the last 32 stage.
Paraguay and Singapore will also compete in the "Mizuho Blue Challenge" from November 13 to 17 during the FIFA international window.
Singapore open the event, to be played at their national stadium, against Paraguay on November 13, with the Japan-Brazil clash the following day.
The tournament ends with a double-header on November 17, when Singapore take on five-time World Champions Brazil before Japan face Paraguay.

item.title: George Clooney awarded Golden Lion for lifetime achievement
item.description:
George Clooney received the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the opening ceremony of the Venice Film Festival on Wednesday.
The Hollywood actor became emotional during the ceremony, with his wife, Amal Clooney, also visibly moved. Clooney received the honor from longtime friend and occasional co-star Laura Dern.
Clooney and Dern first worked together more than 4 decades ago on the horror sequel “Grizzly II: Revenge”, which was filmed in Hungary early in their careers.
The ceremony had an unusual connection to Clooney’s recent film “Jay Kelly”, a comedy-drama about the personal struggles of a movie star. The film ends with its protagonist receiving a lifetime achievement award at an Italian film festival.
“Jay Kelly”, which also stars Dern, premiered at Venice last year. Organizers screened an extended clip from the film during the ceremony, closely echoing the real-life event.
Following a standing ovation, Clooney reflected on his 45-year career and the people who helped shape it.
“I’ve been an actor for 45 years, and when I look back now, it might seem as though I had a carefully mapped-out career, but that was never the case,” he said.
Clooney described his career as “a series of fortunate accidents” and credited the directors, writers, actors and crew members who gave him opportunities.
“No one reaches the top entirely on their own,” he said.
He also spoke about cinema’s ability to connect audiences across cultural and geographical boundaries, saying people share many of the same emotions regardless of language or nationality.
Clooney also addressed threats faced by journalists and artists under authoritarian regimes. He said those who challenge powerful figures and resist simplistic narratives can become targets of attempts to control public discourse.
While acknowledging that films cannot end wars or solve political and economic crises, Clooney said cinema can encourage audiences to empathize with people whose experiences differ from their own.
Clooney’s relationship with the Venice Film Festival dates back decades. Steven Soderbergh’s “Out of Sight” screened at the festival in 1998, helping mark his transition from television actor to major Hollywood star.
He later returned to Venice with films including “Michael Clayton”, “Burn After Reading” and “Gravity”.
The festival also played an important role in Clooney’s career as a director. “Good Night, and Good Luck” premiered in competition at Venice and earned Clooney and Grant Heslov the screenplay prize before receiving 6 Academy Award nominations.
Clooney’s connection with Venice extends beyond cinema. He and Amal Clooney held their wedding celebrations in the city in 2014.
The lifetime achievement tribute was followed by the world premiere of Danny Boyle’s “Ink”, starring Jack O’Connell, Guy Pearce and Claire Foy, which is competing for the Golden Lion.
The festival’s competition also includes titles such as Robert Pattinson’s “Primetime”, Martin McDonagh’s “Wild Horse Nine”, Lee Chang-dong’s “Possible Love”, Hirokazu Kore-eda’s “Look Back” and Florian Zeller’s “Bunker”.
A 7-member jury headed by Maggie Gyllenhaal will select the Golden Lion and other major prizes, with winners scheduled to be announced at the closing ceremony on September 12.

item.title: Netflix announces three-part documentary on Matthew Perry
item.description:
Netflix has announced “The One About Matthew Perry," a three-part documentary series examining the life, career, and legacy of the late “Friends” star. The series will premiere globally on October 27.
Directed by Emmy-winning filmmaker Mary Robertson, the documentary will look beyond Perry’s iconic role as Chandler Bing to explore his rise to fame, personal struggles, and the experiences that shaped his life.
Perry played Chandler across all 10 seasons of "Friends," which aired from 1994 to 2004 and ran for 236 episodes. The role made him one of television’s most recognizable actors.
The series will feature previously unheard accounts from Perry’s sister, Mia Perry Bowick, and lifelong friends, along with unreleased photographs and videos from the Perry family’s private archive.
Creative collaborators and others who were close to Perry will also share their memories of the actor.
The documentary will examine Perry’s long struggle with addiction, a subject he discussed publicly during his later years. He wrote about his experiences with addiction and recovery in his 2022 memoir, “Friends, Lovers, and the Big Terrible Thing."
According to Netflix, the series aims to portray Perry as a person beyond his public image and his best-known television character.
Robertson said Perry’s career brought laughter and a sense of connection to audiences, while his openness about addiction became another significant part of his legacy.
Mia Perry Bowick is among the documentary’s central voices. She has said she wanted viewers to remember her brother as a complete person rather than defining him solely through Chandler Bing or his struggles with addiction.
“The One About Matthew Perry” is produced by Maxine Productions, a Sony Pictures Television company. Robertson also serves as an executive producer alongside Lisa Kalikow, Eli Holzman, and Aaron Saidman. Lora Moftah is the co-executive producer, while Jessica Call serves as producer.

item.title: HBO releases new teaser for Harry Potter series
item.description:
HBO has released a new teaser for its upcoming “Harry Potter” series, offering a first look at the young cast at Hogwarts ahead of the show’s December 25 premiere.
The teaser features Dominic McLaughlin as Harry Potter, Alastair Stout as Ron Weasley, and Arabella Stanton as Hermione Granger. It shows the trio arriving at Hogwarts, taking part in the Sorting Ceremony and beginning their first year at the wizarding school.
The footage also introduces John Lithgow as Albus Dumbledore, Janet McTeer as Professor Minerva McGonagall, Paapa Essiedu as Severus Snape, and Nick Frost as Rubeus Hagrid.
Viewers can also see glimpses of Quidditch, magical lessons, and Harry discovering the Invisibility Cloak, along with scenes connected to the mystery of the Philosopher’s Stone.
The first season will consist of eight episodes and is based on JK Rowling’s “Harry Potter and the Philosopher’s Stone." The series is planned as a seven-season adaptation of Rowling’s seven-book series, with each season focusing on one book.
HBO has already renewed the series for a second season, which will adapt “Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets."
The wider cast includes Lox Pratt as Draco Malfoy, Rory Wilmot as Neville Longbottom, Leo Earley as Seamus Finnigan, Elijah Oshin as Dean Thomas, Warwick Davis as Professor Filius Flitwick, and Sirine Saba as Professor Pomona Sprout.
Francesca Gardiner serves as showrunner, while Mark Mylod is directing multiple episodes. Rowling is an executive producer alongside Neil Blair, Ruth Kenley-Letts, and David Heyman.
The series is being filmed at Warner Bros Studios Leavesden in the UK and follows the original 8-film franchise starring Daniel Radcliffe, Rupert Grint, and Emma Watson as Harry, Ron, and Hermione.
The new “Harry Potter” series will premiere on HBO and stream on HBO Max from December 25, 2026.

item.title: Traffic violations: Two cases filed against Civil Aviation Minister Millat’s vehicle
item.description:
Two cases have been filed against the car used by Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat on charges of violating traffic laws. The two cases filed by the Traffic Division of the Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) carry a total fine of Tk 6,000.

The minister’s car violated traffic laws in the capital’s Kakrail area on Thursday morning. The car was later stopped in front of the Secretariat and cases were filed against it. Traffic Sergeant Sifat Mahmud filed the cases.

Sergeant Sifat told Prothom Alo that the minister’s car violated the lane rules and created an obstruction to normal traffic movement. A traffic police officer on duty then stopped the car. Later, in the presence of senior officials, cases were filed against the car. He said, “I could not believe that a case could be filed against the minister’s car. It is a rare incident.”

Sifat said their control room had also been informed about the incident, and the Special Security Force (SSF) had instructed them to take action. He said the driver of the car also admitted to violating traffic laws.

Several sources concerned said the minister was in the car when the traffic violation occurred. Prothom Alo tried to contact the minister by mobile phone for his comments on the matter. A text message was also sent to his mobile phone later, but no response was received.

According to the traffic police, a total fine of Tk 6,000 was imposed in two cases against the car, with Tk 3,000 for each offence. One case was for creating an obstruction to traffic movement and the other for driving in an unsafe manner.

Sergeant Sifat said that although the cases were filed against the vehicle’s registration number, the driver is responsible for the violation of the law. Therefore, the driver was asked to pay the fines.

The two sections under which the cases were filed

The traffic police said two cases were filed against the car under Sections 87 and 92 of the Road Transport Act, 2018. A fine of Tk 3,000 was imposed in each case.

Section 87 of the law essentially sets out the punishment for violating the provisions of Section 44. The title of Section 44 is “Control of Motor Vehicle Speed”. However, the section does not deal only with violations of speed limits.

Section 44(2) of the law states that a driver must not drive a motor vehicle at a speed exceeding the prescribed limit or drive recklessly.

Section 44(3) states that a driver must not overtake dangerously or in an unauthorised manner on a road or highway, or create any obstruction to the movement of motor vehicles.

Violation of any provision of Section 44 can result in action under Section 87. Under Section 87, the offence is punishable by up to three months’ imprisonment or a maximum fine of Tk 10,000, or both. In the case of a driver, one demerit point may also be deducted from the driving licence.

In the case of the minister’s car, the allegation of creating an obstruction to the movement of the prime minister’s motorcade is related to the provision of Section 44(3).

The other case was filed under Section 92 of the law. This section provides for punishment for violating the general instructions for the movement of motor vehicles prescribed under Section 49.

The first part of Section 49(1) of the law sets out several mandatory instructions for the movement of vehicles on roads. Among them, driving a vehicle in the opposite direction to the prescribed direction is prohibited. At the same time, stopping a vehicle at a place other than the designated location, on the opposite side or in the wrong direction and thereby creating traffic congestion or any other obstruction is also prohibited.

Punishment for violating these provisions in the first part of Section 49(1) is provided under Section 92(1). This section provides for up to three months’ imprisonment or a maximum fine of Tk 10,000, or both. In the case of a driver, there is also a provision for deducting one demerit point.

item.title: ‘No pressure’ behind US aircraft purchases, says Humaiun Kobir
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir said Bangladesh is buying aircrafts from the United States in response to the needs of the aviation sector.

The state minister made the remarks while answering journalists’ questions at the Foreign Ministry on Tuesday.

Asked whether Bangladesh was purchasing aircraft from the United States under pressure or as a continuation of an agreement signed by the interim government, the foreign affairs state minister said, “No, not because of any pressure.”

He said the aircraft were being purchased due to the needs of the aviation sector.

Bangladesh needs to increase the capacity of its aircraft fleet, the state minister said. Otherwise, it would not be possible to open new routes and the country would lose business, he said.

He added that Bangladesh would have to purchase aircraft over the long term if it wanted to increase revenue and passenger numbers as an aviation hub.

Asked whether there was a specific timeline for purchasing the aircraft or whether discussions were still at an initial stage, the state minister said Bangladesh had very good relations with Washington and also maintained good relations with Beijing. He said the government was maintaining an excellent balance in its foreign relations.

Bangladesh to buy more Boeing aircraft from US

The state minister said that among Bangladesh’s bilateral partners, the United States is one of its major development partners. Therefore, Bangladesh would further expand trade and investment with the country. He said more aircraft would be purchased as needed.

The state minister said Bangladesh would need 70 to 80 aircraft, or even more, over the next 10 to 15 years.

He said a policy-level decision had been taken to purchase Boeing aircraft based on the country’s needs.

Bangladesh has agreed to buy more Boeing aircraft from the United States as part of a new agreement. Sergio Gor, the US special envoy for South and Central Asian affairs and ambassador to India, announced this in a post on X on Sunday night.

Sergio Gor also said that US President Donald Trump and Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman have reached an ‘incredible deal’ this week over the purchase of Boeing aircraft. However, Sergio Gor did not mention in his post how many new aircraft Bangladesh plans to purchase from aircraft manufacturer Boeing.
